chunks.title: Using AEM Guides and DITA to build content AI can use
chunks.text: An AI assistant answers from chunks of your content. The cleaner, smaller and better labelled those chunks are, the better the answers. DITA, the Darwin Information Typing Architecture, was designed for exactly this kind of modular content, and Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) Guides adds the enterprise layer around it.

chunks.title: Using AEM Guides and DITA to build content AI can use
chunks.text: Why DITA suits AI. **Topic-based.** Each topic covers one task, concept or reference, which makes it a natural retrieval unit. **Typed structure.** A task topic has defined places for prerequisites, steps and results, so a system can tell a procedure from background reading. **Built-in metadata.** Attributes such as product, audience, platform and version let you filter content before the AI ever sees it. **Reuse.** Content references and key references keep one source of truth, so there is one answer instead of five near-duplicates. **Conditional publishing.** Filter files produce a variant for each product or release from the same source.

chunks.title: Using AEM Guides and DITA to build content AI can use
chunks.text: What AEM Guides adds. AEM Guides is Adobe's DITA-based authoring and publishing solution built on Adobe Experience Manager. Around the DITA standard it provides the operational layer a large team needs: browser-based authoring, review and approval workflows, versioning and baselines, permissions, translation management and publishing to several outputs. Feature details vary by version, so confirm them in Adobe's current documentation.

chunks.title: Using AEM Guides and DITA to build content AI can use
chunks.text: A practical pattern. 1. **Write one-purpose topics** with specific, task-worded titles, such as "Reset the gateway to factory settings". 2. **Fill in metadata** on every topic and map, using a controlled taxonomy for product, version, audience and content type. 3. **Write a real short description.** It doubles as a summary that helps retrieval. 4. **Publish an AI feed** alongside your human outputs: clean, structured text with its metadata, ready for indexing. 5. **Re-index on every approved release** and retire superseded topics so the assistant never quotes an old version.

chunks.title: Using AEM Guides and DITA to build content AI can use
chunks.text: Write for chunks, not pages. An assistant may read one topic with no surrounding context. Avoid phrases such as "as described above", repeat the product name and version where they matter, and keep steps self-contained.

chunks.title: Using AEM Guides and DITA to build content AI can use
chunks.text: Watch-outs. DITA does not fix weak content. A badly written task in perfect XML still produces a bad answer. Very large topics defeat chunking, and inconsistent tagging makes filters unreliable. Governance matters as much as the tool.

chunks.title: Using AEM Guides and DITA to build content AI can use
chunks.text: Takeaway. DITA gives AI the structure and labels it needs, and AEM Guides gives the team the workflow to keep them accurate at scale. Together they turn documentation into a governed knowledge source rather than a pile of pages.

chunks.title: AEM Guides or AsciiDoc and Antora? Choosing a platform for AI-ready docs
chunks.text: Both approaches can feed an AI assistant. The real question is which one fits your organisation's scale, governance needs and authors. Antora, a static site generator that builds versioned documentation from AsciiDoc in Git repositories, is excellent and free. The case for AEM Guides is strongest in larger, regulated or multi-product organisations.

chunks.title: AEM Guides or AsciiDoc and Antora? Choosing a platform for AI-ready docs
chunks.text: What the open-source stack does well. No licence cost and full control of the toolchain. Content lives in Git, so developers use familiar pull requests and reviews. Fast builds, clean versioned sites and no vendor lock-in. AsciiDoc is readable and easy for engineers to learn. For a small team with a technical audience, this is often the right answer.

chunks.title: AEM Guides or AsciiDoc and Antora? Choosing a platform for AI-ready docs
chunks.text: Where AEM Guides is stronger. **Enforced structure.** DITA validates topic types, so the tool guarantees structure. In AsciiDoc it depends on style guides and linting, which is fragile across many authors. **Governance out of the box.** Roles, permissions, review and approval workflows and audit history are part of the platform. In a Git stack you assemble them from pull-request rules and plugins. **Reuse at scale.** Content references, key references and conditional filtering support thousands of topics across many product variants. Includes and attributes in AsciiDoc work well but are harder to govern across repositories. **Translation.** Managed localisation workflows suit teams working with language vendors. **A wider author base.** Browser-based authoring lets subject-matter experts and writers contribute without learning Git. **Ecosystem and support.** Integration with the wider AEM platform, plus vendor support with service levels.

chunks.title: AEM Guides or AsciiDoc and Antora? Choosing a platform for AI-ready docs
chunks.text: The AI angle. Both can produce chunkable, well-labelled content. The difference is enforcement. With AsciiDoc you maintain structure and metadata through conventions and automated checks. With DITA the schema does much of that at authoring time, which matters when many people write for one assistant.

chunks.title: AEM Guides or AsciiDoc and Antora? Choosing a platform for AI-ready docs
chunks.text: Costs to weigh. AEM Guides brings licence, implementation and migration effort, and it needs skilled administration. Open source shifts that cost to engineering time and process discipline.

chunks.title: AEM Guides or AsciiDoc and Antora? Choosing a platform for AI-ready docs
chunks.text: How to choose. Choose Antora if your team is small, technical and Git-native, and your audience is developers. Choose AEM Guides if you have many authors, several products and releases, translation needs, or compliance and audit requirements.

chunks.title: AEM Guides or AsciiDoc and Antora? Choosing a platform for AI-ready docs
chunks.text: Takeaway. Neither tool makes content AI-ready by itself. Structure, metadata and governance do. Pick the platform that lets your team keep those three consistent at your scale.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Datasheet
chunks.text: NovaGate G200 Datasheet Technical specifications Processor: quad-core 1.2 GHz Memory: 2 GB RAM and 8 GB storage Ports: 2 x Ethernet, 1 x RS-485, 2 x USB Power: 12 to 24 V DC, 6 W typical consumption Operating temperature: -20 to 60 degrees Celsius Ingress protection: IP40 Certifications: CE and FCC

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Error Codes
chunks.text: code: E101; meaning: No network link detected; action: Check the Ethernet cable and the switch port. code: E204; meaning: Cloud authentication failed; action: Check the date and time settings and re-enter the cloud credentials. code: E310; meaning: Configuration file is corrupt; action: Restore a saved backup or perform a factory reset.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 FAQ
chunks.text: Q: What is the default IP address? A: The default IP address is 192.168.1.1. Q: Does the gateway support Wi-Fi? A: Yes. It supports 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wi-Fi. Q: Which protocols are supported? A: Modbus TCP, MQTT over TLS 1.3, and BACnet/IP. Q: How long is the warranty? A: The warranty is 3 years from the purchase date.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Installation Guide
chunks.text: NovaGate G200 Installation Guide. Before you begin. Use a 12 to 24 V DC power supply rated for at least 10 W. Mount the gateway on a DIN rail or a wall. The operating temperature range is -20 to 60 degrees Celsius.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Installation Guide
chunks.text: NovaGate G200 Installation Guide. Connect and power on. 1. Connect an Ethernet cable from the LAN port to your network. 2. Connect the power supply. The power LED turns green within 30 seconds. 3. Open a browser and go to 192.168.1.1. 4. Sign in and set a new administrator password when prompted.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Installation Guide
chunks.text: NovaGate G200 Installation Guide. LED states. Solid green means normal operation. Blinking red means no network link. Solid blue means the gateway is in recovery mode.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Release Notes
chunks.text: NovaGate G200 Release Notes. Version 2.4.0 (September 2026). New. MQTT over TLS 1.3 is now supported. The web interface shows cloud connection status on the dashboard.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Release Notes
chunks.text: NovaGate G200 Release Notes. Version 2.4.0 (September 2026). Fixed. Wi-Fi no longer drops after 24 hours of continuous use.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Release Notes
chunks.text: NovaGate G200 Release Notes. Version 2.4.0 (September 2026). Known issue. Firmware rollback from 2.4.0 to 2.2.x requires a factory reset.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Release Notes
chunks.text: NovaGate G200 Release Notes. Version 2.3.2 (June 2026). Fixed a crash when more than 50 Modbus devices were configured.

chunks.title: Reset the NovaGate G200 to factory settings
chunks.text: Reset the NovaGate G200 to factory settings Use a factory reset to restore default settings when you cannot sign in or after a failed update. Back up your configuration first. A reset erases all settings. Power on the gateway and wait for the green power LED. Press and hold the recessed RESET button for 10 seconds. Release the button when the LED turns solid blue. Wait about 2 minutes while the gateway restarts with default settings. The gateway is available again at 192.168.1.1 with default settings.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Troubleshooting
chunks.text: NovaGate G200 Troubleshooting. The web interface does not open. Check that your computer is on the same network as the gateway and browse to 192.168.1.1. If the page still does not load, power cycle the gateway and wait for the green LED.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Troubleshooting
chunks.text: NovaGate G200 Troubleshooting. The LED is blinking red. A blinking red LED means no network link (error E101). Check the Ethernet cable and the switch port, then restart the gateway.

chunks.title: NovaGate G200 Troubleshooting
chunks.text: NovaGate G200 Troubleshooting. The gateway cannot reach the cloud. Confirm that the date and time are correct and that outbound port 8883 is open on your firewall. Wrong time settings cause error E204.
